slides.title: Why we need calculus
slides.html:
Launch

Motion at an instant

Motion at an instant

LaunchA speedometer moment

Average speed is easy; instantaneous speed is not.

Big Idea

A car travels 60 miles in 2 hours — average speed is 30 mph. But what does the speedometer read at exactly 1:00 PM?

That is not an average over time. It is a rate at an instant.

What it means

Instantaneous rate asks how fast something changes at one input value.

Why it matters

This question leads to derivatives and the limit idea.

How to recognize

Words like “at t = 2 exactly” or “at this moment.”

Common mistake

Using a long interval and calling it instantaneous.

How to check

Shrink the interval and see if the average rates stabilize.

slides.title: Position graph s(t) = t² + 1
slides.html:
Visual Investigation

Position vs time

Position vs time

VisualRead the curve

Slope of a secant = average rate on that time interval.

slides.title: Average rate of change
slides.html:
Concept & Definition

Average rate of change

Average rate of change

Definition · Average rate of change on [a, b]
\[\text{Average rate}=\frac{s(b)-s(a)}{b-a}\]

Geometrically: slope of the secant line connecting the two points on the graph.

Units: (output units) per (input unit) — here, meters per second.

Key Point · At t = 2
\[\frac{s(3)-s(2)}{3-2}=\frac{10-5}{1}=5\ \text{m/s}\]

This is the average velocity from t = 2 s to t = 3 s — not the velocity at t = 2.

slides.title: Shrinking the interval — numeric evidence
slides.html:
Visual Investigation

Table of average rates

Table of average rates

VisualLet h → 0

Use both positive and negative h to approach t = 2.

hIntervalAverage rate (slope)
1[2, 3]5
0.5[2, 2.5]4.5
0.1[2, 2.1]4.1
0.01[2, 2.01]4.01
−0.1[1.9, 2]3.9
−0.01[1.99, 2]3.99
AP Checkpoint
From both sides, average rates approach 4. That limiting value is the instantaneous rate at t = 2.

slides.title: Secant → tangent
slides.html:
Visual Investigation

Secant lines approach a tangent

Secant lines approach a tangent

Average rate = 5.00 (secant slope)

What to notice: As h → 0, the secant slope approaches 4.

slides.title: The difference quotient
slides.html:
Concept & Definition

Difference quotient

Difference quotient

Definition · Difference quotient at t = a
\[\frac{s(a+h)-s(a)}{h}\]
  • s(a+h) − s(a) — change in position
  • h — change in time (length of interval)
  • Quotient — slope of secant from a to a+h
Key Point · Preview only
We will formalize “approach” in Section 1.2. Here: shorter intervals → secant slope → instantaneous rate.

slides.title: Worked example: simplify the difference quotient
slides.html:
Worked Examples(t) = t² + 1 at t = 2

Teacher model — follow strategy, algebra, and verification.

Definition · Understand

Find the instantaneous rate at t = 2 by simplifying the difference quotient.

Key Point · Representation

Algebra + table + secant graph all describe the same limiting slope.

Walk through the solution

Step 1. Build: \(\dfrac{s(2+h)-s(2)}{h}=\dfrac{(2+h)^2+1-5}{h}\).

Step 2. Expand: \((2+h)^2+1-5 = 4+4h+h^2\).

Step 3. Simplify: \(\dfrac{4h+h^2}{h}=4+h\) for \(h\neq 0\).

Step 4. Interpret: as \(h\to 0\), the rate approaches \(4\) m/s.

AP Checkpoint
Conclusion: The instantaneous rate of change of s at t = 2 is 4 m/s.
Key Point · Check

Secant slope on [2, 2.01] ≈ 4.01; tangent slope matches 4.

slides.title: Error analysis: plugging in h = 0
slides.html:
Contrast / Error Analysis

Why h = 0 is not allowed yet

Why h = 0 is not allowed yet

Common Mistake

Substituting \(h=0\) gives \(\dfrac{s(2)-s(2)}{0}=\dfrac{0}{0}\), which is undefined.

Why wrong: \(h=0\) means “no interval,” so the difference quotient does not describe a secant slope.

Correct move: simplify algebraically first, then let \(h\to 0\).

slides.title: Practice: interpret a difference quotient
slides.html:
Strategy

Interval in denominator → average, not instantaneous.

AP PracticeTry it first

Choose an answer, then reveal the full reasoning.

Buffalo population \(b(t)\), \(t\) years since 1800. What does \(\dfrac{b(50)-b(0)}{50}\) represent?

Choose your answer

A confuses a rate with a population value. C needs a limit of a difference quotient. D misreads “average over 50 years.” B is correct: average rate on [0, 50].

slides.title: Practice: instantaneous rate setup
slides.html:
Strategy

Instantaneous requires a limiting process, not one finite interval.

AP PracticeTry it first

Choose an answer, then reveal the full reasoning.

Which expression represents the instantaneous rate of \(s(t)=t^2+1\) at \(t=2\)?

Choose your answer

A, D are average rates on one interval. C is position, not rate. B is the definition of instantaneous rate.

slides.title: Exit ticket · 1.1
slides.html:
Exit TicketCheck your learning

Answer each item before revealing.

  1. 1
    State the average rate of \(s(t)=t^2+1\) on \([2,3]\) and interpret it.

    \(\dfrac{s(3)-s(2)}{1}=5\) m/s — average velocity from t=2 to t=3.

  2. 2
    Simplify \(\dfrac{s(2+h)-s(2)}{h}\) and state the instantaneous rate at \(t=2\).

    Simplifies to \(4+h\); instantaneous rate is 4 m/s.

  3. 3
    Why can't we substitute \(h=0\) into the difference quotient before simplifying?

    It gives \(0/0\) — undefined. We need \(h\neq 0\) for a secant slope.

FlowLaunch · Visual · Concept · PracticeToolsStudy mode · Projector · Packet PDF

slides.title: Limits describe approach, not always value
slides.html:
Launch

Near vs at a point

Near vs at a point

LaunchThe language of approach

We care what happens as x gets close to c.

Big Idea

\(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to c} f(x)=L\) describes behavior near \(x=c\), not necessarily at \(x=c\).

What it means

As x approaches c, outputs f(x) approach L.

Why it matters

Limits let us define instantaneous rate and continuity.

How to recognize

Phrase “as x approaches c” or arrow notation x → c.

Common mistake

Assuming f(c) must equal L.

How to check

Compare table values near c from both sides.

slides.title: Reading limit notation
slides.html:
Concept & Definition

Symbol by symbol

Symbol by symbol

Definition · Informal limit
\[\lim_{x\to c} f(x)=L\]
SymbolMeaning
xinput variable
cthe value x approaches
x → cx gets arbitrarily close to c (not necessarily equal)
f(x)output values of the function
Lthe value f(x) approaches
Key Point · Say it aloud

“The limit of f(x) as x approaches c is L.”

slides.title: Four contrast cases
slides.html:
Visual Investigation

Limit vs function value

Limit vs function value

VisualFour possibilities

Same limit language — different graphs.

slides.title: Representation transfer: graph, table, words
slides.html:
Representation Transfer

One idea — four forms

One idea — four forms

TransferConnect representations

AP questions mix all four.

FormStatement for \(\lim_{x\to 3} f(x)=5\)
Symbolic\(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 3} f(x)=5\)
VerbalAs x approaches 3, f(x) approaches 5.
Tablex: 2.9, 2.99, 3.01 → f(x) → 5
GraphBranches near x=3 approach height y=5
AP Checkpoint
None of these automatically imply \(f(3)=5\).

slides.title: Worked example: limit vs f(c)
slides.html:
Worked ExamplePiecewise at x = 3

Teacher model — follow strategy, algebra, and verification.

Definition · Understand

Find \(\lim_{x\to 3} f(x)\) and compare to \(f(3)\) for the piecewise function.

Key Point · Representation

Algebraic rule for x ≠ 3; separate rule at x = 3.

Walk through the solution

Step 1. For x ≠ 3, f(x) = x + 2, so near 3 the outputs behave like x + 2.

Step 2. Compute: \(\lim_{x\to 3}(x+2)=5\).

Step 3. By definition, \(f(3)=10\).

Step 4. Conclusion: limit exists and equals 5, but \(f(3)\neq 5\).

AP Checkpoint
Conclusion: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 3} f(x)=5\) while \(f(3)=10\).
Key Point · Check

Graph would show open circle at (3,5) and filled dot at (3,10).

slides.title: Contrast: common mis-readings
slides.html:
Contrast / Error Analysis

What the limit does NOT say

What the limit does NOT say

Common Mistake

Wrong: “f(3) = 5 because the limit is 5.”

Why: Limits describe approach; \(f(3)\) is read from the definition or filled dot.

Common Mistake

Wrong: “As x approaches 5, f(x) approaches 3” for \(\lim_{x\to 3} f(x)=5\).

Why: The input approaches c and outputs approach L — do not swap numbers.

slides.title: Guided: write the verbal statement
slides.html:
Guided ExampleYour turn

Use Thinking Space first; reveal hints only when stuck.

Thinking Space

Write your setup and first step before opening any hint.

Write a correct verbal interpretation of \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to -1} f(x)=2\).

  • Hint 1: Which number does x approach?
  • Hint 2: Which number do outputs approach?
  • Hint 3: Does this say anything about f(−1)?
✦
Ready to check?Reveal the model solution only after you've written a full attempt.

Solution: As x approaches −1, the values of f(x) approach 2. (We cannot conclude f(−1)=2.)

slides.title: Practice: best interpretation
slides.html:
Strategy

Match input approach with output approach.

AP PracticeTry it first

Choose an answer, then reveal the full reasoning.

Best interpretation of \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 4} f(x)=8\)?

Choose your answer

A confuses limit with value. B,D swap 4 and 8. C is correct.

slides.title: Practice: limit vs value from graph
slides.html:
Strategy

Both statements can be true simultaneously.

AP PracticeTry it first

Choose an answer, then reveal the full reasoning.

\(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 2} f(x)=3\) but \(f(2)=1.5\). Which is true?

Choose your answer

Limit 3 and value 1.5 can coexist (Case B). C is correct.

slides.title: Practice: identify the error
slides.html:
Strategy

Counterexample: piecewise with f(1) defined differently.

AP PracticeTry it first

Choose an answer, then reveal the full reasoning.

A student says: “Because \(\lim_{x\to 1} f(x)=4\), we know \(f(1)=4\) in all cases.” True?

Choose your answer

B is correct. Case B shows limit 5 with f(3)=10. Limits do not force f(c)=L.

slides.title: Optional: ε–δ definition
slides.html:
Optional enrichment
\[\forall\varepsilon>0,\ \exists\delta>0:\ 0<|x-c|<\delta\Rightarrow|f(x)-L|<\varepsilon\]

Precision for “arbitrarily close.” Not required for AP computation at this stage.

slides.title: Exit ticket · 1.2
slides.html:
Exit TicketCheck your learning

Answer each item before revealing.

  1. 1
    Write \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 5} f(x)=-2\) in words.

    As x approaches 5, f(x) approaches −2.

  2. 2
    True or false: \(f(1)=\lim_{x\to 1} f(x)\) in all cases.

    False. Counterexample: removable hole or jump.

  3. 3
    Name two things that can differ when \(\lim_{x\to c} f(x)=L\).

    \(f(c)\) may be undefined or may equal a value different from L.

FlowLaunch · Visual · Concept · PracticeToolsStudy mode · Projector · Packet PDF

Tap a phase or press Next to begin.

slides.title: The four-step graph procedure
slides.html:
Launch

Left → Right → Compare → Value

Left → Right → Compare → Value

LaunchA stable routine

Use the same steps on every graph problem.

Big Idea
  1. Trace from the left — \(x\to c^{-}\)
  2. Trace from the right — \(x\to c^{+}\)
  3. Compare — equal heights → two-sided limit exists
  4. Inspect the filled point — \(f(c)\), only after limits
What it means

Estimate limits by approaching c on each side of the graph.

Why it matters

Graphs appear on every AP exam before algebraic limit rules.

How to recognize

Open circle vs filled dot; left vs right branch heights.

Common mistake

Reading the filled dot before comparing sides.

How to check

Re-trace both branches; label L⁻ and L⁺ before deciding.

slides.title: One-sided limits
slides.html:
Concept & Definition

One-sided limits

One-sided limits

Definition · Left-hand and right-hand limits
\[\lim_{x\to c^-} f(x)=L \quad\text{(from left)},\qquad \lim_{x\to c^+} f(x)=M \quad\text{(from right)}\]

Superscript − means \(xc\).

slides.title: Two-sided limit exists when sides agree
slides.html:
Why It Works

Combining one-sided limits

Combining one-sided limits

Definition · Two-sided limit
\[\lim_{x\to c} f(x)=L \iff \lim_{x\to c^-} f(x)=\lim_{x\to c^+} f(x)=L\]
AP Checkpoint
If left and right limits differ, the two-sided limit does not exist.

slides.title: Worked example: piecewise at x = 2
slides.html:
Worked ExampleRead limits at x = 2

Teacher model — follow strategy, algebra, and verification.

Definition · Understand

Find \(\lim_{x\to 2} f(x)\), \(f(2)\), and continuity at x=2.

Key Point · Representation

Graph: left branch y = x+1, right branch y = −x+5.

Walk through the solution

Step 1. Left trace: as x→2⁻, y→3.

Step 2. Right trace: as x→2⁺, y→3.

Step 3. Compare: both sides → 3, so \(\lim_{x\to 2} f(x)=3\).

Step 4. Filled dot at (2, 1.5) gives \(f(2)=1.5\neq 3\) → not continuous.

AP Checkpoint
Conclusion: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 2} f(x)=3\), \(f(2)=1.5\), not continuous at 2.
Key Point · Check

Open circle at height 3; filled dot at 1.5.

slides.title: Case gallery: continuity types
slides.html:
Visual Investigation

Compare discontinuity types

Compare discontinuity types

slides.title: Worked example: jump discontinuity
slides.html:
Worked ExampleJump at x = 3

Teacher model — follow strategy, algebra, and verification.

Definition · Understand

Determine \(\lim_{x\to 3} f(x)\) from the jump graph.

Key Point · Representation

Use left trace, right trace, compare.

Walk through the solution

Step 1. Left: \(\lim_{x\to 3^-} f(x)=-1\).

Step 2. Right: \(\lim_{x\to 3^+} f(x)=2\).

Step 3. Compare: −1 ≠ 2.

Step 4. Conclusion: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 3} f(x)\) does not exist.

AP Checkpoint
Conclusion: Two-sided limit DNE because one-sided limits disagree.
Key Point · Check

A filled dot at f(3) would not repair the jump.

slides.html:

slides.title: Guided: compare sides
slides.html:
Guided ExampleYour turn

Use Thinking Space first; reveal hints only when stuck.

Thinking Space

Write your setup and first step before opening any hint.

For the jump graph at x=3, find \(\lim_{x\to 3^-} f(x)\), \(\lim_{x\to 3^+} f(x)\), and \(\lim_{x\to 3} f(x)\).

  • Hint 1: Trace left branch to x=3.
  • Hint 2: Trace right branch to x=3.
  • Hint 3: Are the heights equal?

slides.html:

Use Thinking Space first; reveal hints only when stuck.

Thinking Space

Write your setup and first step before opening any hint.

Sketch a graph such that \(\lim_{x\to 2^-} f(x)=3\), \(\lim_{x\to 2^+} f(x)=3\), but \(f(2)=-1\).

slides.title: Practice: jump discontinuity
slides.html:
Strategy

Unequal one-sided limits → DNE.

AP PracticeTry it first

Choose an answer, then reveal the full reasoning.

Left limit 3, right limit 5 at x=b. Which is true?

Choose your answer

C — cannot average 3 and 5. Jump means two-sided limit does not exist.

slides.title: Practice: read piecewise graph
slides.html:
Strategy

Continuity requires limit = value.

AP PracticeTry it first

Choose an answer, then reveal the full reasoning.

On the x=2 graph, \(\lim_{x\to 2} f(x)=3\) and \(f(2)=1.5\). Is f continuous at 2?

Choose your answer

B — limit exists but ≠ f(2). Redefining would be “removing” discontinuity (topic 1.13).

slides.title: Practice: filled dot trap
slides.html:
Strategy

Filled dot gives f(c); limits come from approach.

AP PracticeTry it first

Choose an answer, then reveal the full reasoning.

A student reads f(2)=−1 from a filled dot and concludes \(\lim_{x\to 2} f(x)=-1\). Error?

Choose your answer

B — must trace left and right branches first.

slides.title: Error analysis: skipping a side
slides.html:
Contrast / Error Analysis

Incomplete traces

Incomplete traces

Common Mistake

Mistake: checking only the left branch because it “looks closer.”

Fix: always record both \(L^{-}\) and \(L^{+}\) before deciding.

slides.title: Exit ticket · 1.3
slides.html:
Exit TicketCheck your learning

Answer each item before revealing.

  1. 1
    State the four-step graph procedure in order.

    Left trace → right trace → compare → inspect filled point.

  2. 2
    If \(\lim_{x\to 3^-} f(x)=-1\) and \(\lim_{x\to 3^+} f(x)=2\), does \(\lim_{x\to 3} f(x)\) exist?

    No — one-sided limits differ.

  3. 3
    On the x=2 piecewise graph, find \(\lim_{x\to 2} f(x)\) and \(f(2)\).

    Limit = 3; f(2) = 1.5.
